title: DSM-5: Classification of Neurodevelopmental and Other Childhood Disorders
summary: What DSM-5 is and how it is used, the end of the multi-axial system, and how childhood disorders were reorganised from DSM-IV into new classes.

sections.name: What DSM-5 is and what changed

lesson.title: The diagnostic rulebook
lesson.hook: A child in Ibadan and a child in Chicago with the same symptoms should get the same diagnosis. That only works if clinicians everywhere share one rulebook. For psychiatry, that rulebook is the DSM.

slides.heading: What DSM-5 is
slides.body:
**DSM-5**, short for the *Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders*, 5th edition, is how the **American Psychiatric Association (APA)** classifies mental disorders. (Your notes write 'Psychiatrist'; the body is the American **Psychiatric** Association.)

It was published in **2013** after a **14-year** revision of DSM-IV-TR by many international teams. A text revision, **DSM-5-TR**, followed in 2022.

slides.heading: What it is used for
slides.body:
Clinicians and researchers use the DSM to **diagnose and classify** mental disorders, including **substance use disorders**. For children, a diagnosis weighs the **symptoms**, **how long** they have lasted, and **how much they disrupt** life at home, in school and in the wider community.

Like DSM-IV, it aims to identify disorders that interfere with **normal development**, **relationships with family and peers**, and reaching **developmental milestones**.

slides.question: DSM-5 was published by the American Psychiatric Association in:
slides.why: DSM-5 appeared in 2013 after a 14-year revision; DSM-5-TR followed in 2022.

slides.heading: An evidence-based effort
slides.body:
DSM-5 was a **multinational, interdisciplinary** effort to build a large body of **empirical research** into the classification of mental illness.

Its reclassifications reflect **better understanding** from new research and clinical knowledge, rather than simply renaming things.

terms.meaning: Mental health and substance use disorders
Psychosocial and environmental problems, such as housing or employment

slides.heading: Goodbye to the axes
slides.body:
Perhaps the most visible change in DSM-5 is that the **five-axis (multi-axial) system was scrapped**. DSM-IV had used five axes to organise biopsychosocial information.

DSM-5 lists diagnoses together, with separate notes on medical conditions and psychosocial factors, and drops the GAF score.

slides.heading: One child, two reports
slides.story: Under DSM-IV, a clinic report on 9-year-old Zainab might read: Axis I, ADHD; Axis II, none; Axis III, asthma; Axis IV, parents' recent divorce; Axis V, GAF 55. Under DSM-5, the same report lists ADHD and asthma together, notes the divorce as a relevant stressor, and describes how her functioning is affected, without the axes.
slides.takeaway: DSM-5 keeps the same information but drops the five-axis structure.

slides.question: Under DSM-IV, Axis V recorded:
slides.why: Axis V was the GAF scale; Axis III was medical conditions; Axis II was personality disorders and mental retardation.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'what is DSM-5?', 'what is it used for?' and 'what major change did DSM-5 make?' (the axes were removed). Objectives test what each axis contained. Trap: putting mental retardation on Axis I; it was on Axis II with personality disorders.
slides.sampleQuestion: In DSM-IV, Axis II consisted of: (a) general medical conditions (b) personality disorders and mental retardation (c) psychosocial problems (d) global functioning
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (b). Then state that DSM-5 removed the axes entirely.

points: DSM-5: the American Psychiatric Association's classification, published 2013.
It followed a 14-year, multinational, evidence-based revision.
Used to diagnose and classify mental and substance use disorders.
Children's disorders judged by symptoms, duration and impact across settings.
Key change: the five-axis system was eliminated.

lesson.title: Reorganising childhood disorders
lesson.hook: In DSM-IV, autism, ADHD, conduct disorder and separation anxiety all lived in one big 'childhood' chapter. In DSM-5 they were scattered across different chapters. Why break up the family?

slides.heading: Classes of disorders
slides.body:
Both DSM-IV and DSM-5 group disorders into **classes**, putting together disorders that share **symptoms** or suspected **causes**, to make the manual easier for clinicians and researchers.

In DSM-5, your course notes that **six classes were added** and **four were removed**.

terms.term: Disorders usually first diagnosed in infancy, childhood or adolescence
Mental disorders due to a general medical condition

terms.meaning: Moved into trauma- and stressor-related disorders

slides.heading: Dropped does not mean deleted
slides.body:
'Dropped' means the **class heading** no longer exists, **not** that the disorders inside it disappeared. Most were **recategorised** into other classes.

For children, the biggest change was scrapping the old '**disorders usually first diagnosed in infancy, childhood or adolescence**' chapter. Its disorders now sit in classes organised by **type of problem**, not by **age**.

slides.question: When DSM-5 'dropped' the class of disorders first diagnosed in childhood, the disorders in it were:
slides.why: Dropping a class removes the heading; the disorders were recategorised elsewhere.

left.title: Neurodevelopmental disorders
points: Autism spectrum disorder (formerly pervasive developmental disorders)
ADHD, learning, communication, motor and tic disorders

right.title: Other classes
points: ODD and conduct disorder: disruptive, impulse-control and conduct
Separation anxiety and selective mutism: anxiety disorders
Reactive attachment disorder: trauma- and stressor-related

slides.heading: New classes in DSM-5
slides.body:
New classes include **neurodevelopmental disorders**, **obsessive-compulsive and related disorders**, **trauma- and stressor-related disorders**, and **elimination disorders**.

Old classes were also renamed and split. For example, DSM-IV's '**mood disorders**' became two classes: **bipolar and related disorders** and **depressive disorders**. '**Sexual and gender identity disorders**' split into **sexual dysfunctions**, **gender dysphoria** and **paraphilic disorders**.

slides.heading: Following the disorders
slides.story: A lecturer gives the class a game: find each childhood disorder's new DSM-5 home. Autism goes to neurodevelopmental disorders as autism spectrum disorder; ADHD joins it there. Conduct disorder moves to disruptive, impulse-control and conduct disorders. Reactive attachment disorder lands in trauma- and stressor-related disorders, because neglect is part of its cause.
slides.takeaway: DSM-5 groups childhood disorders by the type of problem and likely cause, not by the age they first appear.

slides.question: In DSM-5, ADHD is classified under:
slides.why: ADHD moved into the new neurodevelopmental disorders class.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'mention four classes present in DSM-IV but dropped in DSM-5', and matching questions on where childhood disorders now sit. Learn the table: neurodevelopmental (intellectual disability, autism, ADHD, learning, communication, motor, tics); disruptive (ODD, conduct); anxiety (separation anxiety, selective mutism); trauma (RAD); elimination; feeding and eating. Trap: putting RAD under anxiety.
slides.sampleQuestion: Mention four classes of disorders present in DSM-IV but dropped in DSM-5.
slides.howToAnswer: Name these four: the old childhood chapter (disorders usually first diagnosed in infancy, childhood or adolescence), mental disorders due to a general medical condition, factitious disorders, and adjustment disorders. Note that their disorders were recategorised, not deleted.

points: Four classes dropped, including the childhood chapter; six added.
Dropped classes' disorders were recategorised, not deleted.
Neurodevelopmental: intellectual disability, autism spectrum, ADHD, learning, tics.
ODD and conduct: disruptive class; separation anxiety: anxiety; RAD: trauma-related.
Mood disorders split into bipolar and depressive classes.

questions.stem: Which pair of childhood disorder and DSM-5 class is correctly matched?

questions.stem: What does it mean that a DSM-IV class was 'dropped' in DSM-5?
options: The class heading was removed and its disorders were mostly recategorised
questions.explanation: Dropping a class does not remove its disorders; they were reclassified.

questions.stem: I. ADHD and autism spectrum disorder are both neurodevelopmental in DSM-5. II. Separation anxiety disorder is neurodevelopmental. III. Elimination disorders became their own class. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and III are correct. Separation anxiety is an anxiety disorder.

questions.stem: What principle best explains DSM-5's reorganisation of childhood disorders?
options: Grouping by type of problem and suspected shared causes
questions.explanation: DSM-5 groups disorders with similar symptoms or causes, regardless of when they first appear.

questions.stem: DSM-IV's 'sexual and gender identity disorders' was split in DSM-5 into:
options: Sexual dysfunctions, gender dysphoria and paraphilic disorders
questions.explanation: The class became three: sexual dysfunctions, gender dysphoria and paraphilic disorders.
